newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Goodale refuses limits on wheat exports.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Goodale refuses limits on wheat exports.

text.p: Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale has rebuffed any idea of reinstating limits on Canadian wheat exports to the United States.
In a statement received on Sunday, Goodale said he was responding to remarks by Charlene Barshefsky in her hearings before the Senate to confirm her as U.S. Trade Representative.

Barshefsky said in her remarks the United States would not tolerate any market disruption from Canadian wheat and barley shipments, it would consult with Canada and it would work towards a long-term agreement on Canadian wheat exports.
Goodale said bilateral talk was fine but limits were not.
Asked what Canada would do in response to any American request for formal consultations on cross-border grain flows, he said:

"If our good trading partner wants to sit down and talk about something, Canada is always willing to have a reasonable discussion, based upon the true facts, but we are not prepared to embark upon any process leading to limitations."
The news release from his department was relaying remarks Goodale made at the weekend to the U.S. National Grain Trade Council at a meeting in Florida.
Goodale noted that with the new World Trade Organization agreement in place, the old law of the jungle had been replaced with a rules-based system applicable to all countries, large and small.
"These days of unilateral trade actions are gone and any new trade measures must be in accordance with agreed multilateral rules," he said.
The minister also challenged the idea that if Canadian sales into the United States continued at their current rate they would set a new volume record and justify limits.
"The Minister also warned against the United States reviving its Export Enhancement Program (EEP)," the statement said.

"EEP subsidies would not only distort market signals to American farmers and lower world prices for everybody, they would also warp the trade between Canada and the U.S. and serve inevitably to increase American imports from Canada," Goodale said.
"The linkage is undeniable. If the U.S. again uses EEP, it will have made the conscious decision to trigger more grain flows from the north."

"This is false. There have been no unusual developments to warrant concern. Canadian wheat and barley continue to be traded fairly, consistent with Canada's trade rights and obligations -- as previous U.S. investigations have repeatedly verified," he said.

The statement said Canadian wheat exports to the United States were indeed higher than a year ago but nowhere near a record and below the pace of 1994-95, in which the U.S. government imposed a one-year import limit on Canadian wheat. Canada was also importing more U.S. wheat and barley. "This is the normal ebb and flow of imports and exports..." it said.
Rather than resorting to the EEP, Goodale called on Washington to work closely with Ottawa in seeking a global end to export subsidies as a farm policy tool.
He said he was constantly "amazed at how narrowly focused lobbyists and short-sighted political spokespersons constantly try to sabotage" the huge two-way agri-food trade.
"We simply must not allow local grievances, unreal misperceptions, faulty communications or the hot breath of political rhetoric to impede our valuable trade flows," he said.
